routing.ruling: Curriculum, not a standalone reference. Twenty-two companion PDFs form one coherent Year 3 program with teaching philosophy, scope, recurring weekly structures, reusable activity formats, and 167 planned instructional blocks across prehistoric science, animal science, nature study, integrated language arts, Profiles in Science Book Seeds, and math through art.
routing.recipeRuling: Every recurring printable or activity format maps to an existing shared Homa recipe. No source artwork, page geometry, copyrighted question set, or publisher-specific visual identity is copied into a recipe.

layer1_philosophy.methodology: Charlotte Mason-inspired, secular, literature-rich, hands-on eclectic curriculum
principles: Use living books, read-alouds, and picture study as anchors for science, literature, geography, biography, mathematics, and art.
Move through Wonder, Explore, and Record: kindle curiosity, offer several hands-on routes, then preserve learning through narration, notebooks, or a portfolio artifact.
Let the parent choose among options according to time, budget, learner interest, local conditions, and available materials.
Prefer oral or written narration, field journals, and portfolios to tests, grades, or one correct worksheet response.
Bring large scientific ideas close to home through nature observation, local ecosystems, scavenger hunts, and open-ended projects.
Use each Profiles in Science Book Seed as a two-week interdisciplinary study built around one or two living biography books.
Teach visual mathematics through a three-part loop: picture study, an explicit math concept, and process art.
Protect curiosity and confidence by allowing rabbit trails, flexible pacing, adaptation, and exploration without pressure for a perfect product.

evidence.quote: hands-on activities, projects, demonstrations, and experiments
student notebook to employ written narration
develop confidence, not to attain perfection

layer1_philosophy.parentRole: facilitator, read-aloud partner, discussion guide, resource curator, project helper, and scribe when needed

knowledgeBankMatches.note: The existing row covers living books, narration, nature study, picture study, short lessons, and portfolio assessment. This bundle adds a distinct publisher format but does not require another philosophy row.

knowledgeBankGaps.title: Blossom & Root Year 3 format
knowledgeBankGaps.summary: A secular Year 3 bundle combining 13 prehistoric wonders, 36 animal-science wonders, 40 nature-study projects and prompts, 36 integrated language-arts weeks, six two-week Profiles in Science Book Seeds, and 36 art-math picture studies. The recurring design is literature first, hands-on exploration, narration or notebook recording, and flexible parent choice.

knowledgeBankGaps.title: Profiles in Science Book Seed format
knowledgeBankGaps.summary: A two-week interdisciplinary unit anchored by one or two illustrated scientist biographies, then expanded through science, mathematics, art, nature study, writing, recipes, dramatic play, and optional family extensions for ages six through twelve.

layer3_structure.cadence: A 36-week core year with parallel weekly animal science, integrated language arts, nature study, and math-through-art options, plus a 13-wonder prehistoric extension and six Book Seeds designed for roughly two weeks each.
layer3_structure.cadenceEvidence: Aim to complete one unit per week, in order
layer3_structure.weeklyTemplate: Language arts uses a five-day rhythm: divide the read-aloud across the week and read independently daily; use Monday for copywork and word play, Tuesday for geography, Wednesday for story elements, vocabulary, and dictation, Thursday for narration and a literature project, and Friday for journaling, a bonus activity, or a creative extension. Science uses Wonder, Explore, Record. Art-math uses picture study, math concept, and art exploration. Nature study chooses one prompt or continues a long project.
layer3_structure.progressionModel: Parallel linear strands with flexible entry, optional rabbit trails, and portfolio accumulation. The prehistoric and animal-science sequences are chronological or taxonomic; language arts moves through ten whole works; art-math moves from solids to symmetry, visual density and texture, color, graphs, ratios, and scale.
layer3_structure.reviewRhythm: Daily read-aloud and independent reading, weekly narration and journaling, recurring nature notebook entries, repeated Wonder-Explore-Record cycles, and notebook or portfolio review instead of periodic tests.
layer3_structure.durationEvidence: one unit per week, in order, for a 13-week period

activityTypes.description: Book-centered packets that connect science, mathematics, writing, art, nature, recipes, and play.
activityTypes.sourceQuote: Using inspiration from beautiful and captivating children's literature selections

activityTypes.description: Stepwise art exploration tied to a featured artist, natural material, scientific idea, or mathematical concept.
Open observation, sketching, tracking, measurement, and reflection in a nature notebook.
A child retells learning orally or in writing, with a parent acting as scribe when useful.
Short handwriting and visual transcription practice drawn from the week's literature.
Write a heard word, phrase, or sentence, then compare it with a separate parent key.
Open discussion prompts about character, setting, plot, theme, vocabulary, and viewpoint.
Sort animals, adaptations, habitats, words, or traits into meaningful categories.
Label or construct a visual model of animal anatomy or biological structure.
Collect visual or observed data and represent it in a chart or graph.
Sequence key events, places, discoveries, and obstacles in a scientist's life.
Observe, hide, recall, and discuss a featured artwork before making art.
Record core ideas, vocabulary, observations, or a brief response after exploration.
Manipulate words, roots, prefixes, suffixes, and vocabulary through hands-on word play.
A compact set of optional projects and extensions around one literature or science focus.

recipeAudit.result: all recurring activity mechanics are covered by current reusable recipes

layer5_lessons.notes: This 22-file bundle contains six independent numbering systems. The first digit of each stored ordinal is a bundle-only namespace: 1 prehistoric wonder, 2 animal-science wonder, 3 nature project or prompt, 4 language-arts week, 5 Book Seed issue, and 6 art-math week. The source's own number remains in the suffix and in the verbatim unit label. All 167 planned blocks are decomposed, not sampled.

questions.text: A Midsummer Night's Dream is a play. A play is a piece of literature, mostly made of dialog (or talking between characters or to the audience) and usually intended to be performed for an audience rather than read privately by a single reader. Some plays have only a single character or narrator. Some plays have many characters. A Midsummer Night's Dream is a play with many characters. When we're reading the story of the play (as we did this week) or reading the play itself, it is helpful to get a clear idea of the characters first. Can you name some of the characters in the story?

questions.text: Many authors breathe life into their characters by telling us very specific things about them. They might reveal to us a favorite movie (like Star Wars in our book), a meaningful memory or story from their past (like the story of the "farting nurse" and Auggie's birth), or a favorite holiday (like Halloween for Auggie.) These can help us to feel like we really know them, or like they are "real people" because we can imagine these details in our mind's eye and because we can relate--most of us have a favorite movie, a favorite story about when we were little, a favorite holiday, and so on. Literature Project: The Art of the Detail Invent a character in your mind. Spend time really seeing them in your imagination. Once you have a clear picture, begin filling in the details. What's their favorite food?

questions.text: All of the books (and the play) we've read so far have a common theme. A theme is an important message, idea, or lesson in a work of literature or art. The theme they all have in common is the idea of wonder. But "wonder" has many meanings. It can mean curiosity. It can mean something strange, unexpected, or unusual. It can mean questioning or pondering. And it can mean something beautiful and complicated--a miracle. Think of the different ways "wonder" has come into the literature we've read so far. What did it mean in Alice's world?

questions.text: There are so many ways to tell a story: a novel, a picture book, a play, a movie, a piece of art, a song, a puppet show, a dance, a comic book, or just telling one out loud around a campfire. This story is told in the form of a graphic novel. A graphic novel looks like a regular book on the outside, and like a regular book they tell a full-length story (or a series of small, connected stories) with characters and settings and points of view and plots. But they're different from a regular book in one major way: instead of just words, they have panel- style illustrations that do a large part of the storytelling. Cece Bell, the author of El Deafo, decided to use a graphic novel format to tell her story. Can you imagine how it might be different if she'd told it in a regular story format, or a play?

questions.text: An author may have many reasons for wanting to share a story. Sometimes, it's an idea they've been working on for years and years. Sometimes they are inspired by another story, work of art, or song. Sometimes they write a story because they want to learn and share more about a certain period in history. And sometimes an author decides to share their own story--experiences that happened to them. El Deafo is based on author Cece Bell's own experiences, and her own life. We call that an autobiography. If you were going to write a story about something that happened to you, what would it be about?

questions.text: Sometimes, authors will tease or hint at things to come with a little sprinkle or a wink. In our book, Christopher Paul Curtis (the author) begins the book with Part One: "...Gang Aft A-Gley..." In chapter five, Mrs. Needham recites a line from the poem that this phrase comes from. The poem, "To a Mouse," was written by Scottish poet Robert Burns after he accidentally plowed over a mouse's home, destroying it. In the poem, he understands that this is devastating for the mouse, that may not survive the winter without its home. The poem says, "the best laid schemes o' mice and men gang aft a- gley." In other words, "the plans we think are going to happen may not work out, no matter how carefully we made them." Do you think the author is giving us a hint about what's coming in the book?

questions.text: Alliteration and other word play is prominent throughout our story. Alliteration is especially fun! When we string a bunch of words together that all begin with the same letter or the same sound, that's alliteration. Roscoe's names for his family members are a great example of alliteration: "Darling Daughter Deza," "Dearest Delightful Daddy," "Jimmie the Genuine, Gentle Jumpin' Giant," "Fine Friendly Father Figure," and "Mother the Marvelous Mammalian Matriarch." And of course we can't forget her mother's name for Roscoe, "hardheaded husband who hasn't heard how horrible he is." Alliteration can be playful and fun. It can make words seem like music, and make it easier to remember things. That's why many companies also use alliteration in their names and mottos. (Dunkin' Doughnuts, Coca-Cola, Krispy Kremes, etc.) Literature Project: Alliteration Play with alliteration this week. Make up names for your own family members and pets, invent brand names and slogans, or simply slip them into your daily conversations to add some playfulness to the day. "Mama, may you move the milk my way?

questions.text: One of the most important jobs for an author is to set the scene for the reader. Think of the worlds we've explored in books this year--they are all so different. And now we have arrived in the Yorkshire moors--a different world altogether. How does the author, Frances Hodgson Burnett, bring that world to life for us, right from the beginning?

decisionsNeeded.item: RESOLVED: audited all 15 recurring activity types against current Material Studio recipe files, the Format library, and the activity-format registry. Copywork and dictation now route separately, and word-play-cut-and-sort aliases to the existing cut-and-paste-word-work recipe.
